statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women in general go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men (the idea called 'telescoping'): the faster course was described mostly in people in treatment and self-help groups, from ages they recalled years later; the general-population survey read here for alcohol did not find the full pattern; and in a US general-population survey of cannabis use disorder, read in full, the recalled time from first use to the disorder was 0.40 years shorter in women, among people who already had the disorder and without adjustment for age, not the 2.5 years a critique reports. In two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, response 90%, and NESARC, 2001–2002, response 81%; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57; every age recalled at a single interview), women had their first drink later than men (on average at 19.0 against 17.8 years; the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943 to 0.4 years in those born 1974–1983). Among the 38,309 lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks ever), men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence than women in every birth cohort (hazard ratios 1.36 to 1.79, adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age). The authors read these hazards, the survival curves and a significant interaction of cohort, gender and time (its estimates not shown) as men becoming dependent faster, especially in younger cohorts. In the editors' reading, a hazard among all drinkers combines the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, and because the average times below were similar, the higher hazard in men mostly reflects that more men became dependent (in the table's unweighted counts, 23.7% of male and 16.2% of female lifetime drinkers; editors' arithmetic). Among the people who did become dependent, the group whose timing treatment-sample studies measure, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years; unadjusted); it was shorter in women born 1964–1973 (3.7 against 4.2 years) and, not marked significant, in those born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4), and longer, not significantly, in women of the other three cohorts. Among people with dependence, men also had a higher hazard of first alcohol treatment, significantly in two of five birth cohorts (1.55 and 1.42) (Keyes et al., 2010). The authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population, although their Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither measure goes further than their own table. As described in a historical critique, the idea goes back to a 1952 WHO committee report and to stage models built from the recalled drinking histories of 98 men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with 15 women's answers set aside; the phrase 'telescoped development' was first used in 1958; the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term asked 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups to recall four landmark ages, and the interval from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter on average in the women; 75 of 103 articles citing that study used it as background without testing it; and the critique's authors recommend dropping the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). The same critique describes a US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, without giving its timing measure or adjustment (Marks & Clark, 2018); read in full, the survey shows a much smaller difference, and the critique misreports both the difference and the sample. In NESARC 2001–2002 (43,093 US adults interviewed once, response 81%), the comparison was restricted to the 2,080 men and 1,217 women (3,297 in all) who had ever had DSM-IV cannabis abuse or dependence: they had first used cannabis at the same average age (16.71 against 16.73 years) and the disorder had begun at similar ages (19.34 against 18.98 years, not significant), and the recalled time from first use to the disorder was 2.64 years in men and 2.24 in women, a difference of 0.40 years, about 5 months (p = 0.026). The comparison was adjusted neither for current age, although the women with the disorder were younger, nor for anything else; it was one of about 50 comparisons made without correction (editors' count on the study card); and it describes speed among people who developed the disorder, not who develops it: the authors cite another analysis of the same survey in which 11.8% of men and 5.4% of women had ever had the disorder. The authors present the 0.40 years as evidence of telescoping outside treatment (Khan et al., 2013). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids, but not heroin, found mainly in women already in treatment, and, following an earlier review, explains the difference from population surveys by who is sampled: women in treatment likely have more severe disorders (McHugh et al., 2018; its cannabis citation points to a general-population paper on alcohol dependence). The same group's earlier review states as established that women advance faster from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, citing six studies, among them treatment samples and one population survey (Dawson, 1996) that the review itself describes elsewhere as showing no earlier treatment entry for women (Greenfield et al., 2007). The treatment-sample study that the papers above describe in opposite ways, read in full, compared people entering a US alcohol treatment trial (Project MATCH, 1991–1993, nine sites; 379 women and 1,210 men with all four landmark ages, recalled at entry; women and men compared within study arm and fifth of current age, nothing else adjusted for): women recalled first getting drunk regularly, first alcohol problems and first difficulty stopping drinking 2.5 to 3.9 years later than men (getting drunk regularly at 26.6 against 22.7 years on average) but reached their worst period of drinking at the same age (35.2 against 35.0 years). The recalled intervals were shorter in women from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 against 2.3 years) and from loss of control to the worst period (5.5 against 7.8 years), not from first problems to loss of control (2.3 against 2.2 years), and, among the 735 people for whom the trial was their first treatment, from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 against 15.8 years). Gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance; the differences were small or absent in the youngest fifth of participants (average age 26.6; getting drunk regularly at 18.8 against 18.0 years) and grew with age; and only 53% of participants reported the landmarks in the order the intervals assume. Women and men entered treatment at about the same ages (38 to 42 years on average), so a later start in women by itself shortens every interval that ends at treatment: women started getting drunk regularly 3.9 years later than men and reached first treatment 4.2 years sooner after that (editors' comparison), and in the editors' approximate reading of the paper's figure the gaps in time to treatment by age group (about 0.8 to 7.7 years) track the gaps in the age of getting drunk regularly (0.8 to 7.1 years). The authors call telescoping relatively robust in people seeking treatment and recommend alerting women in general that they are more likely to develop alcohol problems rapidly (Randall et al., 1999); the papers that cite the study as showing telescoping, and the critique that counts it among studies with fewer telescoping effects, are each partly right. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Do women go from first use to problems faster than men? This has not been shown for women in general. The idea, called 'telescoping', came mostly from small groups of people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous, who had to remember years later when each step happened, and its stages were first drawn from men's stories. In two big US surveys of adults in the general population, women had their first drink later than men, and fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol. Among the people who did become dependent, women got there about as fast as men, on average about 6 years after their first drink, and a little faster in one age group. The survey's authors read their results as men getting there faster; the editors think this mostly shows that more men became dependent. In a big US survey, among people who had had a cannabis use disorder, women and men had started cannabis at the same age, about 17, and the women's disorder began on average about 5 months sooner after their first use (2.2 against 2.6 years); a review reported this as 2.5 years, which is wrong. In a US alcohol treatment study, women started getting drunk regularly about 4 years later than men but reached their worst drinking at the same age, about 35, so the steps in between looked shorter; the differences were small and grew with age, and because women and men came into treatment at about the same age, a later start alone makes the time to treatment look shorter. A review suggests that the women who reach treatment may have more severe problems, which would explain why a faster course shows up in treatment. All these studies relied on memory. See the contested question.
population: Adults in two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES 1991–1992 and NESARC 2001–2002; US-born, aged 18 to 57; 53,238 people, 38,309 of whom were lifetime drinkers, with more than 12 drinks ever) for alcohol; US adults with a lifetime cannabis use disorder in NESARC 2001–2002 (2,080 men, 1,217 women); people entering a US alcohol treatment trial (Project MATCH, 1991–1993; 1,210 men, 379 women); and, for other drugs and other treatment and self-help samples, studies described in a historical critique and two narrative reviews
exposure: Being a woman (the studies compare by gender and do not separate sex from gender)
outcome: Time from first use, or from early drinking landmarks, to later landmarks, dependence or use disorder, and first treatment ('telescoping'), every step recalled at one interview or in questionnaires
magnitude: Not estimable as a general difference in speed. General-population surveys, alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010): age at first drink, women 19.0 vs men 17.8 years (gap 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943, 0.4 in those born 1974–1983; editors' subtraction); hazard of dependence among all lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks), men vs women, 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for people born 1974–1983, 1964–1973, 1954–1963, 1944–1953 and 1934–1943 (a mixture of the chance of dependence and its speed, read by the authors as faster progression in men; whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently); share of lifetime drinkers with a time to dependence in the unweighted Table 1 counts, men 23.7% vs women 16.2% (4,631 of 19,549 and 3,121 of 19,263; editors' arithmetic; these counts total 7,752, against 8,564 people with dependence in the hazard analysis); mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted), women 5.6 vs men 5.8 years (ratio 1.04, not significant), born 1964–1973 3.7 vs 4.2 years (p = 0.02), born 1954–1963 5.5 vs 6.4 years (not marked significant; t about 2.4 from the printed means and standard errors, an editors' approximation on the study card), and longer in women in the other three cohorts (3.1 vs 2.8, 8.6 vs 7.9 and 11.8 vs 10.4 years; none marked significant); hazard of first treatment among people with dependence, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58) and 1.38 (0.84–2.26) in the same cohort order; mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated, born 1934–1943, women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years (the overall means, 6.1 vs 7.0, cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows and are not used). Treatment and self-help samples, second-hand (Marks & Clark, 2018): the 1989 study credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men, first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter in women, first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later in women, same age at treatment entry; Iowa treatment centres (3,132 men, 395 women), treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit in women, about 3 in men; 75 of 103 citing articles used the 1989 study as background. General-population survey of cannabis use disorder as described by Marks & Clark (2018): first use to the disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, in 1,217 women and 3,297 men; read in full (Khan et al., 2013; NESARC 2001–2002; 2,080 men and 1,217 women with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse or dependence, 3,297 in all), men vs women, weighted means (SE): age at first use 16.71 (0.10) vs 16.73 (0.12), p = 0.88; age at onset of the disorder 19.34 (0.13) vs 18.98 (0.16), p = 0.10; time from first use to onset 2.64 (0.10) vs 2.24 (0.13) years, F = 5.20, p = 0.026, a difference of 0.40 years (approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72, editors' calculation on the study card), unadjusted, among people with the disorder; lifetime disorder in the whole survey, cited by the authors from another analysis, 11.8% of men vs 5.4% of women. Treatment sample, read in full (Randall et al., 1999; Project MATCH 1991–1993; 379 women, 1,210 men; compared within study arm and fifth of current age), women vs men, mean (SD) recalled age at getting drunk regularly 26.6 (10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96), first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87), loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95), worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93); intervals, drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04), first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67) years; drunk regularly to first treatment, 735 people in their first treatment (numbers of women and men not reported), 11.6 (9.01) vs 15.8 (9.67) years, F(1, 715) = 44.5; gender ω² .01 to .04; youngest fifth of current age, drunk regularly 18.8 vs 18.0 years, oldest fifth 37.8 vs 30.7.

risk_of_bias.note: Every timing was recalled at a single interview or in questionnaires, years or decades later (card sc_keyes_2010: JBI, moderate); treatment samples select people by having reached treatment: the one read in full (card sc_randall_1999: JBI, high for this question) recruited people at treatment entry at similar ages, which by itself shortens women's intervals ending at treatment, and its effects were small, while the others are known here only through reviews that did not appraise them (cards sc_marks_2018, sc_mchugh_2018, sc_greenfield_2007); the cannabis survey (card sc_khan_2013: JBI, moderate) compared only people with the disorder, without adjustment for age, among about 50 uncorrected comparisons; in the survey analysis the hazards among all drinkers mix the chance of dependence with its speed, the averages among people who became dependent are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently, and several table and text values disagree.

inconsistency.note: Treatment samples point towards a faster course in women, and the general-population cannabis survey towards a slightly shorter one (0.40 years) among people with the disorder, while the general-population alcohol analysis does not find the full pattern; within the survey paper, the hazards (read by the authors as men faster) and the averages among people who became dependent (no difference overall; women faster in one cohort) differ; a review, following an earlier one, explains the difference by sample, which is plausible but untested.

indirectness.note: The general-population analyses read concern alcohol (US-born adults aged 18 to 57 interviewed in 1991–1992 and 2001–2002) and cannabis (US adults with the disorder in 2001–2002, from one of the same surveys), and the one treatment sample read in full concerns alcohol in the USA in 1991–1993; the evidence for other drugs (cocaine, opioids, heroin) and from other treatment samples is second-hand (narrative reviews; METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: The survey estimates are precise (at least 4,603 people per cohort); the small treatment samples (33 women in the 1989 study) are part of the second-hand evidence already rated down; the treatment sample read in full has 379 women (66 to 85 per fifth of current age) and does not report how many of the 735 in its treatment comparison were women; the cannabis difference has an approximate 95% CI of 0.08 to 0.72 years (editors' calculation on the study card).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; that 75 of 103 papers citing the 1989 study used it without testing it concerns citation, not publication.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low, the floor. Counted once: McHugh et al. (2018) updates Greenfield et al. (2007) by the same group and reuses its search; both reviews and the critique describe overlapping treatment-sample studies and the same general-population analysis (Keyes et al., 2010), so they add no independent data; the survey analysis pools NLAES, which Greenfield et al. also cite through Dawson (1996), and NESARC, which is also the source of the cannabis analysis (Khan et al., 2013), so the two survey analyses share respondents, for different drugs; the treatment study now read (Randall et al., 1999) is the one Keyes et al., McHugh et al., Greenfield et al. and Marks & Clark cite, so their descriptions of it add nothing independent. Each figure is labelled with its quantity: hazards among all drinkers (chance and speed together, read by the authors as speed) or averages among people who reached the step (speed only); that the hazards mostly reflect the chance of becoming dependent is the editors' reading, resting on the similar average times and on Table 1's unweighted counts, and the claim gives the authors' reading beside it. Reading Randall et al. (1999) and Khan et al. (2013) in full weakened the yes side without removing it: the treatment-sample differences are small (gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance), small or absent in the youngest participants and partly produced by recruiting both sexes at treatment entry at similar ages; the cannabis difference is 0.40 years among people who already had the disorder, unadjusted for age, with no difference in the age at which the disorder began, and the critique's 2.5 years misreports it. The certainty stays very low. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways (treatment samples, and a small difference among people with the disorder in a general-population cannabis survey, against the general-population alcohol survey), with a published critique of the concept, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Do women go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men, or does the faster course seen in treatment samples come from who reaches treatment and from how the timing was remembered?
debate.evidence_yes: The faster course was described mostly in people in treatment. In the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups recalled their landmark ages: the women had started drinking about 2 years later and had first been drunk about 3 years later, entered treatment at the same age, and went from their first alcohol-related problem to their first treatment 4.3 years faster on average; in an earlier Iowa treatment sample (3,132 men and 395 women), women reached treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit and men about 3 (as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). In the treatment sample most often cited, read in full (Project MATCH, 1991–1993; 379 women and 1,210 men entering alcohol treatment), women recalled shorter intervals from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 against 2.3 years) and from loss of control to their worst period of drinking (5.5 against 7.8 years), and, among people in their first treatment, from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 against 15.8 years); the authors call telescoping relatively robust in people seeking treatment (Randall et al., 1999). Outside treatment, in a US general-population survey (NESARC 2001–2002), among the 2,080 men and 1,217 women who had ever had a cannabis use disorder, the recalled time from first use to the disorder was shorter in women (2.24 against 2.64 years, p = 0.026), which the authors present as telescoping (Khan et al., 2013; a narrative review's citation for cannabis points to a different paper). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids (McHugh et al., 2018), and the same group's earlier review states faster progression to first treatment as established for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence (Greenfield et al., 2007). In the general-population alcohol surveys, among the people who did become dependent, women born 1964–1973 got there faster than men (on average 3.7 against 4.2 years), the printed figures suggest the same for women born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4 years, not marked significant; an editors' approximation on the study card), and among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010).
debate.evidence_no: In the general-population analysis read for alcohol, two pooled US national surveys (1991–1992 and 2001–2002; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57), women started drinking later than men, but among the lifetime drinkers men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence in every birth cohort (1.36 to 1.79) and, among people with dependence, a higher hazard of first treatment (significant in two of five cohorts, 1.55 and 1.42), after adjustment for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink (and, by the table's footnote, age); the authors read the dependence hazards as men progressing faster, especially in younger cohorts. Among people who became dependent, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years) and, in three of five cohorts, longer in women, not significantly; the authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population (Keyes et al., 2010). A narrative review, following an earlier one, explains the gap between treatment samples and population surveys by who is sampled, since women who reach treatment likely have more severe disorders, and reports that telescoping was not found for heroin (McHugh et al., 2018). The historical critique shows that the stages that define telescoping were drawn from the recalled histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous (98 men analysed, 15 women's answers set aside), that the 1989 study was small and drawn from treatment and self-help settings, and that 75 of 103 papers citing it used it as background without testing it; it argues that, with women as the reference group, men's longer course might have been called magnification, and recommends discarding the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). Read in full, the two studies most cited for the yes side show less than their citations suggest. In the treatment sample, gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance, the differences were small or absent in the youngest fifth of participants, women reached their worst period of drinking at the same age as men (35.2 against 35.0 years), and both sexes entered treatment at about the same age, so women's shorter intervals largely mirror their later start (Randall et al., 1999). In the cannabis survey, women and men had started cannabis at the same age (16.73 against 16.71 years) and developed the disorder at similar ages (18.98 against 19.34 years, not significant); the 0.40-year difference was not adjusted for age although the women were younger, describes only people who developed the disorder, and appears in the critique as 2.5 years (Khan et al., 2013; Marks & Clark, 2018).
debate.neither_can_show: Every timing in these studies was recalled, often decades later, at a single interview or in a questionnaire; none was recorded as it happened, and no study read tested whether women and men remember timing differently (the surveys' recall check, which the authors read as showing limited recall bias, tested only whether dependence beginning at 25 or later was reported less often by members of the same birth cohorts interviewed 10 years later). Treatment samples time only people who reached treatment, so a group that reaches treatment soon after its problems begin will look fast whatever its course in the population, and when women and men are recruited at treatment entry at similar ages, a later start in women by itself shortens every interval that ends at treatment. Comparisons restricted to people who developed a disorder, as in the cannabis survey, show speed among them, not who develops it. In the general-population surveys, hazards among all drinkers combine the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, so on their own they cannot say who is faster; the averages among people who became dependent come closer to speed but are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, and the youngest cohort, interviewed only as young adults, could contribute only early steps. People who died before the surveys, or were older than 57, are missing. None of these designs separates sex (biology) from gender (roles, access to treatment, stigma); the general-population evidence read is for alcohol and cannabis in the USA only.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The faster course in women was described mostly in small treatment and self-help samples, from recalled ages, and the idea grew out of stage models built from men's recalled histories. In the general-population survey read for alcohol in the USA, women were less likely than men to become dependent and, once dependent, had a lower hazard of reaching treatment, and those who did become dependent got there about as fast as men on average, faster in one birth cohort; the authors read the same data as men progressing faster, a reading that rests on hazards that mix the chance of dependence with its speed and on an interaction whose estimates are not shown. So the evidence read here does not show that women in general move faster from first use to dependence; whether women who do develop dependence move faster, and whether this holds for other drugs, is open. Read in full, the two studies that bear most directly on the yes side show less than their citations suggest: in the alcohol treatment sample, women's shorter recalled intervals were small overall, small or absent in the youngest participants, and partly produced by recruiting both sexes at treatment entry at similar ages (Randall et al., 1999); in the cannabis survey, the difference was 0.40 years among people who had developed the disorder, unadjusted for age, with no difference in the age at first use or at onset of the disorder, not the 2.5 years a critique reports (Khan et al., 2013).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young women and men followed from before first use, with use, dependence criteria and treatment recorded as they happen (repeated interviews or linked records), analysed with methods that separate the chance of ever becoming dependent from the speed of progression among those who do (for example mixture-cure or competing-risks models), with sex (including hormonal status) and gender (roles, access to treatment) measured separately; and a systematic review of telescoping studies, drug by drug, that separates treatment from general-population samples and recalled from prospectively recorded timing.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether drinking at a young age causes alcohol problems in adulthood, or whether the same family, genetic and personal factors lead to both. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected people took part), the 27,616 adults who had ever drunk were asked how old they were when they first started drinking, not counting tastes or sips: lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence was reported by 40.6% to 47.3% of those who recalled starting at 14 or younger, 16.6% of those who started at 18 and 7.9% of those who started at 25 or older (with a rise to 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24), and lifetime abuse without dependence by up to 13.8% (a first drink at 14) against 2.5% (25 or older). After adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history of alcoholism, duration of drinking and current or former drinking, the odds of lifetime dependence were 14% lower, and of abuse 8% lower, for each later year of the first drink, with no confidence intervals or unadjusted estimates given. The age of the first drink was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses, often decades later; conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, family environment and other drug use were not measured; two of the adjustments (current or former drinking, and the duration of drinking up to the last drink) may themselves follow from the disorder; and people who had died, were in institutions or were homeless were not sampled. The authors call the age of the first drink a powerful predictor and ages 16 and younger a particularly vulnerable period, but their closing paragraph says that the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors may explain the link and that a prospective study is needed to tell (Grant & Dawson, 1997). In general-population cohorts that recorded the age of the first drink during adolescence, an earlier first drink went with more adult drinking or alcohol problems in some analyses and not in others, and the association often shrank when other risk factors were taken into account. A systematic review found only four such cohorts up to January 2013 (two in the USA and two in Norway; 447 to 1,311 people each; five reports; no meta-analysis; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card): in an Oslo school cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21, with control only for parents' and peers' influence; in a US community cohort, a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, depending on where the first drink happened, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) but not after adjustment for further risk factors, while feeling drunk at the first drink remained a predictor; in the Young in Norway cohort, drinking by 13 to 14, compared with a later first drink, went with frequent intoxication (odds ratio 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9) and with an AUDIT score of 8 or more, a screen for risky drinking (1.6, 1.3 to 2.1), at 26 to 27, adjusted for gender, both falling to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) when conduct problems in adolescence were also taken into account; in a Seattle cohort of people who started drinking before 21, the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with alcohol dependence at any follow-up, but, compared with a first drink at 11 to 14, a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the interviews held every 3 years from 21 to 33 (odds ratio 1.68) and, in a later report, with more chronic dependence, essentially unchanged across four adjusted models. The review's abstract says that rigorous adjustment markedly weakens or removes such associations, which its own Seattle summary contradicts; the authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems, and found that feeling drunk at the first drink and the start of regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In a Minnesota cohort of twins born 1977 to 1984 (1,512 twins at about age 11; drinking reported at the assessment planned for age 14, held at a mean age of 14.8; outcomes at about 25), twins who had drunk without their parents' permission by that assessment already differed beforehand from twins who had not, notably in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; after weighting for 29 characteristics of the twins and their families measured at about 11, early drinking was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score (standardized coefficient 0.57, SE 0.06), and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking the association was a little over a third as large but remained (0.21, SE 0.09, in all pairs; 0.22, SE 0.10, in identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family; the estimates for identical and fraternal pairs did not differ significantly), whereas within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14) (Irons et al., 2015). Twin comparisons remove what co-twins share, not differences between them such as their own early use of tobacco or other drugs. The same survey's analysis for other drugs is in the answer on starting to use drugs young (Grant & Dawson, 1998). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does drinking young lead to alcohol problems later? This is not known. In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who remembered starting to drink at 14 or younger had had alcohol dependence at some time, against 8 in 100 of those who started at 25 or older; but they were remembering back many years, and the survey could not tell whether early drinking itself, or something that leads to both, explains the link. In the few studies that followed young people over time, in the US and Norway, drinking early went with more drinking problems as an adult in some studies, but in others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems in adolescence, were taken into account. Feeling drunk at the first drink and starting to drink regularly went with later problems more strongly than the age of the first drink. In US twins, the twin who had drunk without their parents' permission by about age 15 drank more as an adult than the twin who had not, even in identical twins, though the difference was smaller than when all the young people in the study were compared; in identical twins, early drinking was not clearly linked to later symptoms of an alcohol disorder. Twin studies cannot rule out other differences between twins, such as smoking or other drug use. See the contested question.
population: US adults who had ever drunk alcohol, in a 1992 national household survey (27,616), recalling their first drink; and young people in general-population cohorts followed from adolescence into adulthood: four cohorts in the USA and Norway in a systematic review (447 to 1,311 people each) and Minnesota twins born 1977–1984 (1,512 at about age 11)
exposure: An earlier first drink: in the survey, the recalled age at which drinking started, not counting tastes or sips; in the cohorts, a first drink (more than a few sips; definitions differed, from before 11 to by 13–14) recorded in adolescence; in the twin study, drinking without parental permission, or being intoxicated, by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8)
comparator: People who started drinking later (in the survey, by each later year of age; in the Rutgers cohort, a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering; in the Seattle cohort, a first drink at 11 to 14); in the twin study, twins who had not, including their own co-twin
outcome: Lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence and abuse reported at the survey interview, at 18 or older; adult drinking, alcohol problems and alcohol dependence in the cohorts and twins (consumption indices, problem scales, AUDIT, DSM-IV symptom counts or diagnoses, at 18 to about 33)

risk_of_bias.note: The 1992 survey recalled the age of the first drink in the same interview as the diagnoses, measured none of the main shared causes except family history of alcoholism, and adjusted for two variables that may follow from the disorder (card sc_grant_1997: ROBINS-E, high); the cohorts adjusted for different, incomplete sets of confounders (only one for family history; none for genetic liability), some possibly on the causal path; confidence in the review is critically low (card sc_maimaris_2014: AMSTAR 2, no protocol, no list of excluded studies, single-reviewer screening); in the twin study, confounders not shared by co-twins, such as their own early tobacco or drug use, were not measured, and 12% were not seen at about 25 (card sc_irons_2015: ROBINS-E, some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The association survived adjustment in some analyses (the 1992 survey, with limited adjustment; Seattle chronicity; within twin pairs for adult drinking) and not in others (Rutgers, Young in Norway, Seattle misuse and any dependence; identical pairs for abuse or dependence symptoms).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one US national survey (1992), four cohorts in the USA and Norway and one Minnesota twin cohort, with outcomes from drinking scores to symptom counts and chronic dependence, all stated.

imprecision.note: The survey is large but gives its per-year estimates without intervals; cohorts of 447 to 1,311 people with small exposure groups (a first drink before 11); no intervals for the Seattle estimates; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs (editors' estimate on the study card), with standard errors close to the estimates.

publication_bias.note: The review judges publication bias a profound threat but could not test it; not rated down separately, since the certainty is already at its floor.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low, the floor. Counted once: the two Seattle reports share one cohort (four cohorts, not five studies). The twin study's printed p-values are not valid (card reporting issue), so significance is judged from coefficients and standard errors. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the association of an earlier first drink with more adult drinking in several cohorts is reported in it, not rated as a separate claim. Grant & Dawson (1997), the cross-sectional survey usually cited as the starting point, read in full, adds a steep association between a recalled early first drink and lifetime dependence (40.6% to 47.3% for a first drink at 14 or younger against 7.9% at 25 or older; 14% lower adjusted odds per later year); it describes what US adults reported in 1992 but cannot separate cause from shared liability, as its authors say, so the certainty about cause does not change. The same survey's analysis for other drugs (Grant & Dawson, 1998) is in the answer on starting drugs young. Status contested: credible analyses point both ways and the review's own authors say the answer is not known, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does drinking at a young age cause alcohol problems in adulthood, or do the same family, genetic and personal factors lead both to early drinking and to later problems?
debate.evidence_yes: In a 1992 US national survey of 27,616 adults who had ever drunk, lifetime alcohol dependence was reported by 40.6% to 47.3% of those who recalled a first drink at 14 or younger against 7.9% of those who started at 25 or older, and the odds of dependence were 14% lower for each later year of starting after adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history of alcoholism, duration of drinking and current or former drinking (Grant & Dawson, 1997). In the Seattle cohort, a first drink before 11 went with more chronic alcohol dependence to age 33, and the association was essentially unchanged after adding peer, school, behavioural and substance-use factors in four models (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted), with none of the three alternative explanations tested supported; in the Oslo cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21 (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In Minnesota twins, drinking without parental permission by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8), recorded at that assessment, was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score after weighting for 29 childhood characteristics (0.57) and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking (0.21), including identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family (0.22, SE 0.10); across all discordant pairs it was also associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.24, SE 0.11). The authors read the within-pair results as supporting an effect of early drinking, while noting that confounders not shared by co-twins could explain them (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.evidence_no: In two of the four general-population cohorts the association did not survive adjustment: in the Rutgers cohort a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) only before adjustment for further risk factors, and in the Young in Norway cohort drinking by 13 to 14 went with frequent intoxication and risky drinking at 26 to 27 (1.5 and 1.6, adjusted for gender) only until adolescent conduct problems were taken into account (both 1.2, 0.9 to 1.6); in the Seattle cohort the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with dependence at any follow-up; the Oslo estimate controlled only for parents' and peers' influence; feeling drunk at the first drink and starting regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink; and the review's authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). The authors of the 1992 survey themselves say that other factors associated with an early start more likely explain its link with later disorders, and call for a prospective study to tell whether an early start is a risk factor that can be changed or a marker (Grant & Dawson, 1997). In the twin study, twins who drank by the assessment planned for age 14 already differed beforehand in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; for the adult alcohol-use score the within-pair association was a little over a third of the weighted one (0.21 against 0.57, ratio 0.37; editors' calculation); and within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14), nor was intoxication by that assessment across all pairs (0.29, SE 0.15) (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.neither_can_show: No randomized evidence exists, since the age of a first drink cannot be assigned at random. A survey that asks adults to recall their first drink in the same interview as their diagnoses can show how strong the association is in the population surveyed, but not what causes it, and it misses people who died, were in institutions or were homeless. The cohorts recorded the first drink in adolescence, which avoids recalling it decades later, but they can adjust only for what they measured: only one adjusted for family history of alcohol problems, none controlled for genetic liability, and adjusting for peers or behaviour that early drinking may itself change can remove part of a real effect. In two of the four cohorts the first drink of late starters was not recorded in adolescence or 3 years before the outcome. Co-twin comparisons remove everything twins share (all genes in identical pairs, half in fraternal pairs, and the family they grew up in) but not what differs between them, such as their own early smoking, other drug use or friends, and random error in reporting early drinking shrinks within-pair estimates on its own; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs, so a non-significant result there is not evidence of no effect. Both twin exposures were yes-or-no, so nothing is known about how much the young people drank.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). An earlier first drink goes with much more lifetime alcohol dependence in a large US survey that relied on recall, and with more adult drinking in several cohorts, and part of that link reflects differences that were there before the first drink, such as behaviour problems and family drinking: in two of four cohorts the link disappeared after adjustment, and in twins it was a little over a third as large within pairs as in the comparison weighted for childhood characteristics. Within identical twins, early drinking still went with more adult drinking, which leaves room for an effect of early drinking itself, but it was not clearly linked to symptoms of alcohol use disorder, and the twin design cannot exclude differences between co-twins. The evidence read here cannot say whether delaying the first drink would reduce adult alcohol problems; in the review, feeling drunk at the first drink and early regular drinking were more strongly linked to adult problems than the age of the first drink.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Pooled analyses of identical twin pairs who differ in early drinking across several twin registries, large enough to estimate effects on alcohol use disorder precisely, with early drinking recorded repeatedly (age, amount, intoxication) and the twins' own earlier behaviour and substance use measured; harmonized analyses of several large birth or school cohorts with the first drink recorded as it happens and the same confounders; and natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person, such as changes in minimum legal drinking ages.
